Learning Objectives
Discuss the epidemiology, etiology, and risk factors associated with anterior cruciate ligament
injuries.
Describe the common mechanisms of anterior cruciate ligament injury.
Review the current injury prevention literature and define the biomechanics associated with
anterior cruciate injury mitigation.
Explain the obstacles associated with applying injury prevention/mitigation with respect to
athlete/coach compliance, program fidelity, and adherence.

The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is a crucial stabilizer of the tibiofemoral joint. It prevents
anterior translation of the tibia on the femur and tibial torsion during weight-bearing activities.
The ACL works collectively with the posterior cruciate ligament to stabilize the knee during
dynamic movement. The medial collateral ligament and the lateral collateral ligament are
extracapsular ligaments and, in combination with the ACL, provide stability to the knee joint in
the frontal plane during varus and valgus loading.1
he ACL is one of the most commonly injured ligaments of the knee. Injuries predominantly
occur in a young and physically active population. Many patients have substantial disability
and impairment after an ACL injury. The injury leads to alteration in the kinetics and
kinematics of the knee.2 This biomechanical deficit may lead to an increased risk of
concomitant injury to the meniscus, collateral ligaments, and articular cartilage. The incidence
of osteoarthritis is directly correlated with meniscal injury/involvement.3

Background
ACL injuries often result in instability, pain, joint effusion, altered biomechanics, muscle
atrophy and weakness, and decreased functional performance. ACL injuries often lead to
loss of an entire competitive season or more of sports participation among youth,
collegiate, and professional athletes.2 ACL injuries also are associated with deleterious
long-term clinical sequelae that often include meniscal tears, osteochondral lesions and
an increased risk of early-onset posttraumatic osteoarthritis.4,5
Overview
ACL rupture is a severe ligamentous knee injury, leading to functional instability in the short
term and degenerative joint disease in the long term. Injury to the ligament may lead to
prolonged absence from work and sports activity and may initiate the early onset of
degenerative osteoarthritis.6
The ACL is at highest risk for injury during activities that require pivoting, decelerating, or
landing from a jump during participation in sports, such as soccer, basketball, football, skiing,
and volleyball.7,8


Overview
The number of ACL injuries in the United States has doubled in the past two decades.
After sustaining an ACL injury, the longitudinal risk of osteoarthritis is substantially
increased.9-11 In a study assessing damage to the articular cartilage after ACL injury,
cartilage thickening, particularly in the medial femorotibial compartment and in younger
subjects, was observed more than 5 years after ACL injury. Major perturbations in
cartilage homeostasis were observed over the first 2 years after ACL rupture, with
simultaneous subregional thinning and thickening occurring within the same cartilage
plate or compartment. Interestingly, ACL reconstruction does not appear to mitigate risk
to the articular cartilage or subchondral bone.9
Epidemiology
An estimated 150,000 to 200,000 ACL injuries occur annually in the United States, with an
estimated financial cost of more than $2 billion.12-14 Almost 45,000 of these injuries occur in
children younger than 18 years.15
ACL injuries may be associated with a concomitant injury to the menisci, the articular cartilage,
subchondral bone, and the medial and lateral collateral ligaments.16

Epidemiology
Agel et al17 investigated the rate of ACL injury in collegiate athletes participating in
National Collegiate Athletic Association sports. ACL injuries in females exceeded those in
male counterparts by a factor of three. Most ACL injuries in females occurred via a
noncontact mechanism of injury (60%) versus a contact mechanism of injury for men
(59%). The highest mean annual rate of ACL injury for men was found in football (0.17
per 1,000 athlete-exposures). Women continue to sustain ACL injuries at higher rates
than men in the comparable sports of soccer, basketball, and lacrosse (Resource 1).

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The ACL originates from the posteromedial corner of the medial aspect of the lateral femoral
condyle in the intercondylar notch. This femoral attachment of the ACL is on the posterior
portion of the medial surface of the lateral condyle, posterior to the longitudinal axis of the
shaft of the femur. The attachment site is an interdigitation of collagen fibers and rigid bone in
the transitional zone of fibrocartilage and mineralized fibrocartilage.18,19
The ACL is composed of multiple types of collagen bundles (predominantly type I) and a matrix
made of a collagen network of proteins, glycoproteins, elastic systems, and
glycosaminoglycans.20, 21

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The ACL has two component bundles, the smaller anteromedial bundle (AMB) and the
larger posterolateral bundle (PLB), named in accordance with the bundles’ insertion sites
into the tibial plateau.22 The AMB is taut during knee flexion, and the PLB is taut during
knee extension. In extension, the AMB and PLB are parallel. During knee flexion, the
femoral insertion site of the PLB moves anteriorly as the AMB and PLB form a cruciate
(crossing). As this occurs, the AMB tightens and the PLB loosens (Figure 1).

Figure 1 Schematic drawings of the knee show the anteromedial (AM) and posterolateral
(PL) macroscopic bundles of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). A, The PL bundle (blue)
is tighter than the AM bundle in extension; however, it is less isometric than in flexion. B,
The AM bundle (red) is tighter than the PL bundle in flexion. (Reproduced from Marom
N, Burger J, Pearle AD: Cruciate ligament injuries, in Azar FM, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge
Update: Sports Medicine, ed 6. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2022, pp 193-204.)
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The most common ACL injury mechanism of injury is noncontact in nature. Approximately 70%
of ACL injuries do not involve direct contact to the knee.12 This mechanism of injury is most
commonly associated with sudden deceleration, pivoting, cutting, change of direction, and
landing maneuvers.23-25 These injuries typically occur as the athlete is reacting or
maneuvering in a defensive manner.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:21 AM
AAOS | Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Prevention
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004084
5/19

Contact ACL injuries account for 30% of ACL injuries. These injuries typically involve an
extrinsic, lateral application of force resulting in a valgus/abduction moment of the knee joint.
Females tear their ACLs at a rate of two to eight times that of their male counterparts.26

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
ACL injuries are consistently associated with excessive anterior shear force at the
proximal end of the tibia. This is a major contributor to ACL loading, whereas knee
valgus (peak knee abduction) and tibial internal rotation moments may increase ACL
loading if an anterior shear force at the proximal end of tibia is applied. In addition,
decreased knee and hip flexion, strong quadriceps muscle contraction (in comparison to
decreased hamstring/gluteal contraction), a fixed foot, foot pronation, or increased
posterior ground reaction forces may increase the risk to the ACL.27
Risk Factors
ACL injury is multifactorial in nature. Five categorical risk factors have been identified in ACL
injuries: anatomic, genetic, environmental, hormonal, and neuromuscular/biomechanical;28
however, evidence suggests that these risk factors should not be considered in
isolation29 (Resource 2).
Risk factors are considered to be intrinsic (non-modifiable) or extrinsic (modifiable).30

Risk Factors
Intrinsic risk factors include prior ACL injury, patient age, generalized and specific knee
joint laxity, intercondylar notch width (ratio of notch width to the diameter and cross-
sectional area of the ACL), ovulatory and luteal phases (associated with increases in
estrogen and progesterone) in athletes who are not taking birth control, physiologic
levels of relaxin hormone, decreased hamstring and gluteal strength and recruitment (in
relationship to quadriceps strength), central and peripheral fatigue, altered
neuromuscular control, decreased core strength and proprioception, decreased hip and

9/3/26, 7:21 AM
AAOS | Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Prevention
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004084
6/19

knee flexion angles, high dorsiflexion of the ankle during sports tasks, lateral trunk
displacement and hip adduction combined with increased knee abduction moments
(dynamic knee valgus), and increased hip internal rotation and tibial external rotation
with or without foot pronation.29,31-33 Potential extrinsic noncontact ACL injury risk
factors include dry weather, ambient temperature, surface type, and friction coefficient
(type of shoe/cleat and interaction with playing surface).34-36
Anatomic risk factors include knee-joint geometry, anthropometric differences, knee-
joint laxity, body composition and mass, and lower extremity structural alignment.
Athletes with an ACL injury often present with small cross-sectional area and volume,
increased lateral posterior-inferior tibial plateau slopes, and decreased femoral notch
width indexes.37-39 Elevated body mass in combination with increased joint laxity has
been associated with increased ACL injury risk.40-42
DNA sequence variants have been increasingly associated with genetic susceptibility to
ACL rupture. Genetic predispositions for ACL injury have been investigated. A study on
adolescent alpine ski racers found a substantially greater proportion of parental ACL
injuries in the ACL injured group compared with the uninjured group.43 The presence of
collagen gene variants (COL1A1 and COL12A1) has been correlated with an increased risk
of ACL injury in males and females.44,45 Matrix metalloproteinase genes, which play an
important role in tissue remodeling, may be associated with ACL injury.46 The presence
or absence of polymorphisms of proteoglycan genes also are associated with an
increased risk of ACL injury.47
Environmental risk factors associated with increased noncontact ACL injury risk are dry
weather conditions, decreased precipitation before the match, artificial turf, increased
friction coefficient between the footwear and the playing surface, and equipment
choices (particularly ski and boot selection in alpine skiing).48-51
Neuromechanical and biomechanical risk factors have been well analyzed and include
kinematic and kinetic analysis and understanding the magnitude of muscular activation
and force production. The role of neuromechanical risk factors in ACL injury has been
well studied to recognize the role that high-risk movement patterns play in ACL injury.

Cadaver model studies, biomechanical analysis, cortical control and motor learning, and
neuromuscular deficiency have been examined.52,53
Recent studies have analyzed mechanisms of injury in male and female soccer players to
further delineate the specific kinetics and kinematics directly involved in the mechanism
of injury. Video analysis of male and female athletes with an ACL injury revealed that
high-risk positioning most commonly associated with the sport was associated with
defensive playing positioning with the involved player at or near full hip and knee
extension.23-25 The continued delineation of the risk factors associated with ACL injury
will better clinicians’ ability to elucidate and refine a comprehensive intervention
program to effectively decrease the injury rate in sports.
Injury Prevention
Injury prevention must be addressed from a biomechanical, physiologic, socioeconomic,
psychological, and ease of implementation perspective.
Injury prevention programs (IPPs) targeted at reducing the risk of ACL injury have been
reported in the literature. Although a number of risk factors for ACL injury have been
proposed, biomechanical risk factors have been examined in sufficient depth to support the
design and evaluation of IPPs.
Most IPPs attempt to alter dynamic loading via neuromuscular and proprioceptive training.
The studies that have focused on biomechanics have resulted in a substantial reduction of ACL
injury; however, the studies vary widely in their approach to injury prevention and the validity
of the study design. Most studies to date have been nonrandomized, and very few studies
have been conducted as randomized, controlled trials.
Regardless, a number of common elements tie these programs together. Most include one or
more of the following: strengthening, awareness of high-risk biomechanical positions,
technique modifications, aerobic conditioning, sports-specific agility, proprioceptive and
balance training, and plyometrics.
In-season use of the IPP, in contrast to preseason or offseason use of the IPP, increases the
efficacy of the program.
The most notable ACL IPPs include Sportsmetrics, Prevent Injury and Enhance Performance
Injury Prevention, the 11+ (Figure 2), HarmoKnee, and the Knee Injury Prevention Program.

Diagram shows the 11+ injury prevention program, was developed by an international group
of experts based on their practical knowledge with different injury prevention programs for

amateur players aged 14-years or older. It is a complete warm-up package and should replace
the usual warm-up before training. The package has three parts with a total of 15 exercises.
These exercises should be performed in the specified sequence at the start of each training
session. Part 1, Running exercises at a slow speed combined with active stretching and
controlled partner contacts. Part 2, Six sets of exercises focusing on core and leg strength,
balance, and plyometrics/agility, each with three levels of increasing difficulty. Part 3, Running
exercises at moderate/high speed combined with planting/cutting movements. A key point in
the program is to use the proper technique during all of the exercises. Athletes should pay full
attention to correct posture and good body control, including straight leg alignment, knee-
over-toe position, and soft landings. (Reproduced with permission from Fédération
Internationale de Football Association (FIFA): The “11+” Manual: A Complete Warm-up
Programme to Prevent Injuries. Zurich, Switzerland, FIFA Medical Assessment and Research
Centre (F-MARC), 2007. Available at: https://www.fifamedicalnetwork.com/wp-
content/uploads/cdn/11plus_workbook_e.pdf. Accessed July 12, 2021.

Injury Prevention
The topic of ACL injury reduction and prevention, namely in the female athlete, has been
well investigated for more than three decades.54-60 Most of these neuromuscular
training programs include various strengthening, plyometric, and agility-based drills that
address the major deficits most commonly associated with female athletes who sustain
an ACL injury.61,62 Several programs have been designed as dynamic warm-up programs
to increase implementation fidelity, adherence, and compliance, in addition to
capitalizing on the improved joint-position sense found as a component in well-designed
neuromuscular training warm-up programs.63,64
The Sportsmetrics IPP substantially improved lower extremity muscle strength and
hamstrings-to-quadriceps ratio, decreased landing forces, decreased knee moments,
improved lower limb alignment, and improved balance scores.65 The Prevent Injury and
Enhance Performance IPP substantially improved lower extremity muscle strength and
hamstrings-to-quadriceps ratio, decreased valgus knee moments, improved lower limb
alignment, and increased knee flexion angles.66-68 The 11+ IPP has substantially
improved hip kinematics, decreased overall injury rates across multiple sports,

AAOS | Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Prevention
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004084
10/19

decreased ACL injury rates, and improved overall lower extremity strength ratios.69-72
Programs used during the season have been shown to be associated with higher rates of
efficacy then programs that used during the offseason or during preseason. In addition,
using an IPP before competition has been shown to increase efficacy compared with
days the program is not used.59
In addition, the cohesive and consistent implementation of injury prevention and
reduction protocols may be considered a viable and cost-effective option to reducing the
rate of ACL injury.73 This knowledge can provide critical insight to help improve existing
IPPs and secondary prevention strategies.
Compliance and Program Adherence
The role of compliance in IPPs has been well documented in the literature.59,64,74 Current
research has demonstrated an inverse relationship between injury rate and time loss because
of injury with compliance to the IPPs.56,74
The scientific medical community continues to struggle with consistency in implementation,
program fidelity, and therapeutic compliance. Studies have analyzed the manner in which
different program delivery systems affect compliance and the rate of injury.75 Nations, such as
the United States, Canada, and many regions of Asia and Africa are confronted by a large
geographic expanse with regard to efficient and feasible medical delivery and public health
messaging.
The concept of using instructional DVDs, online streaming resources, and smartphone
applications may offer a cost-effective alternate delivery system for IPPs if a skilled medical
professional is unable to be present.75

Compliance and Program Adherence
Surgeons must understand the reason that compliance is less than optimal (eg, why
coaches, teams, players, and parents opt in or out of a scientifically vetted IPP). Despite
the fact that IPPs have been shown to substantially decrease the ACL injury rate, the
complete public health benefit will not be fully appreciated if such interventions are not
SEND FEEDBACK

followed.73 Therefore, encouraging coaching and player motivation toward
implementing injury prevention methodology into their training repertoire may have
important public health ramifications and positive socioeconomic effects on the
aforementioned cohorts.
Mark as Complete
